steps.body: Temperatures, tides, daylight hours — anything that cycles fits y = a sin(bt) + d (or its −cos twin). The data hands you two of the dials immediately: a day running from 10° up to 30° has **amplitude (30 − 10)/2 = 10** and **midline (30 + 10)/2 = 20**.

dials.feedback: The swing is wrong. Amplitude is half the distance between the high and the low.
The centre is wrong. The midline is the average of the high and the low.

widget.prompt: Daily temperature runs between 30° and 10°. Build the model with the dials.
widget.successFeedback: Amplitude 10, midline 20: half the 20-degree spread, centred on their average. Every wave-fitting problem starts with these two — (high − low)/2 and (high + low)/2 — before any period work begins.
widget.lowFeedback: The wave does not yet run between 10 and 30.
widget.highFeedback: The wave now swings past the 10-to-30 range.

explanationVariants: midline = (30 + 10)/2 = 20° — the temperature the day oscillates around.
Check: 20 ± 10 rebuilds the 30° high and 10° low. ✓

widget.prompt: Same data (high 30°, low 10°). What is the midline?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 is the amplitude — the swing. The midline AVERAGES the extremes: (30 + 10)/2 = 20.
40 is the sum before halving — the average needs the divide: 20.

steps.body: The third dial comes from the real-world REPEAT time: **b = 2π/period**, exactly as in the graphs chapter — except now the period arrives in hours or seconds. A tide repeating every 12 hours takes b = 2π/12 = π/6 ≈ 0.52.

widget.prompt: A tide repeats every 12 hours. What is b in its model y = a sin(bt) + d? (Round to hundredths.)

commonErrors.feedback: 12 is the PERIOD itself — b is the speed derived from it: 2π/12 ≈ 0.52.

explanationVariants: b = 2π/40 ≈ 0.16 — one full 2π cycle spread over 40 seconds.

widget.prompt: A ferris wheel completes one rotation every 40 seconds. What is b in h(t) = 25 − 20 cos(bt)? (Round to hundredths.)

commonErrors.feedback: 40 is the rotation TIME — the period. b converts it to speed: 2π/40 ≈ 0.16.
251.33 is 40 × 2π — the factor ran the wrong way. Divide: 2π/40 ≈ 0.16.

steps.body: Assembled, the model PREDICTS: plug in a time, get a value. h(t) = 3 sin(πt/6) + 5 models the tide — at t = 3 hours the inside is π/2, sine hits its peak 1, and the tide reads 3 · 1 + 5 = 8 ft: high tide, right on schedule.

widget.prompt: For h(t) = 3 sin(πt/6) + 5, find the tide height at t = 3 hours, in feet.

commonErrors.feedback: 5 drops the sine term — but at t = 3 the inside is π/2, where sine peaks at 1: h = 3 + 5 = 8.
6.5 uses sin(π/6) = 0.5 — the inside is π·3/6 = π/2, not π/6: h = 8.

explanationVariants: Inside: π·20/20 = π; cos π = −1, so h = 25 + 20 = 45 ft — the top, half the 40 s rotation in.
b = π/20 makes the period 2π/(π/20) = 40 s — t = 20 is the half-turn.

widget.prompt: For h(t) = 25 − 20 cos(πt/20), find the rider's height at t = 20 seconds, in feet.

commonErrors.feedback: 5 ft treats cos as +1 — that's t = 0 (or t = 40, a full lap). At t = 20 the inside is π: the TOP, 45 ft.
25 ft treats cos π as 0 — that's the quarter-turn value. cos π = −1, so h = 45.

takeaways: Data gives a and d: half-span and average of the extremes.
Real repeat time gives b = 2π/period — hours and seconds welcome.
The finished model predicts: evaluate the inside first, then swing and shift.
steps.teaser: One tool remains — the identity hiding inside the unit circle since Chapter 3.

concept.body: Two reads, one dataset. A pond's depth cycles between 9 ft and 1 ft. Amplitude = (9 − 1)/2 = 4 — half the span, the swing. (The midline would be the average, 5.) Difference for the swing, sum for the center — keep the two reads straight.

widget.prompt: Depth cycles between 9 ft and 1 ft. What is the amplitude?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 is the MIDLINE — the average (9 + 1)/2. The amplitude halves the difference: 4.
8 is the full span 9 − 1 — the amplitude is half of it: 4.
